version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of page allocation in defrag_mode to make retries follow the promoted order, rather than the original request order. This change is intended to prevent indefinite retrying by requests that are not movable, which can lead to reclaim storms and excessive memory pressure. The patch treats promoted requests as costly orders, resetting progress counters for them and checking compaction results at the promoted order. It also resets retry counters when a fallback attempt is taken, allowing it to get a full retry budget before the OOM killer is considered. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory pressure in systems with high inode churn under memory.low protection.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author agrees that the cleanup changes are redundant and will be folded into the original patch, indicating no further revision is needed.

The author is addressing Johannes Weiner's concern about the effectiveness of the promoted path in reducing reclaim storms. The author built a reproducer to test the patch and found that it significantly reduces reclaim storms, with no measurable difference between the two floors (priority floor and COMPACT_SUCCESS retry limit).

Author acknowledges that the extra SYNC_FULL passes do not provide benefits in this specific workload and agrees to remove them.

The author is addressing a concern about the behavior of defrag_mode in certain scenarios, specifically when I/O is removed and tmpfs is used. They mention that every exhausted order-0 refill does a whole-zone SYNC_FULL pass before falling back, which increases PSI and slows down churn. The author asks for a preference on how to handle this situation, indicating they don't have a strong opinion either way.
review_comments.raw_body:
Will fold it into the fix itself. The cleanup changes the same places as
the fix. It makes zero sense to keep it separate.

---

I built a reproducer around what we saw in production, which was oomd
killing the workload on sustained PSI, so PSI and the number of times
ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT gets dropped are the headline numbers. 32G VM, 8 CPUs:

 - fill memory with 4K anon pages in a cgroup, memory.low = fill + 1G,
   so page cache beyond that stays reclaimable;

 - pin one page in every pageblock with io_uring registered buffers[1],
   except one block in 50 (2%), so whole blocks can be made but only
   from a few places. Without the pins rc5 does not storm in 180s:
   compaction makes 130-210 blocks per run and every retry loop ends in
   one. The storm needs blocks to be hard to produce, and the pin
   fraction is the knob for that;

 - free one page in eight so ~4G sit scattered in movable blocks;

 - turn on defrag_mode and run 8 build-like workers on btrfs for 180s:
   write 1-64K files, read earlier ones back, unlink 20%, fdatasync
   every 50 creates.

Kernels: v7.3-rc5; the fix as posted; the fix with the priority floor
and the COMPACT_SUCCESS retry limit on the requested order. Three runs
each, mean  stddev, 2% producible:

                            rc5            posted        requested
    ops/s                   4751  684     5181  18     5206  84
    PSI some, mean %        28.7  11.5    22.0  0      22.0  0
    PSI some, peak avg10    42.8  30.7    24.9  0.3    25.0  0.8
    s with some avg10 > 50  3.3  5.8      0             0
    give-ups (NOFRAG off)   0              222  58      277  199
    movable blocks lost     641  13       654  10      652  14
    whole blocks claimed    90  8         81  10       76  8

rc5 stormed in one of its three runs: 3.85M order-9 reclaim runs in
180s, PSI at 42% with ten seconds above 50, workers that would not die
on SIGKILL. The other two were quiet, which matches a workload that
OOMs regularly rather than always. The fixed kernels never stormed.

Between the two floors there is no difference I can measure here: same
PSI, same throughput, same give-ups, same movable blocks lost, same
whole blocks produced.

The promoted path is a small part of what the allocator does in this
workload, 16-22k order-9 reclaim runs against a million order-0 ones for
page cache, and a few hundred give-ups in 180s.

---

Same movable blocks lost and same whole blocks produced in all three
kernels, so in this workload the extra SYNC_FULL passes neither produce
blocks nor save any.

---

That shows up only when I take the I/O out: tmpfs, every block pinned,
1M empty files. Then every exhausted order-0 refill does a whole-zone
SYNC_FULL pass before it falls back, PSI some runs at 39% against 20%,
and the churn takes 1.3-2.8x as long, five runs each.

What do you prefer here? I don't have strong preference either way.

[1] One thing the pins made me notice. A FOLL_LONGTERM pin migrates
    the page first only for ZONE_MOVABLE, CMA and isolated blocks, see
    folio_is_longterm_pinnable(); a page in a MIGRATE_MOVABLE block in
    ZONE_NORMAL is pinned where it sits, and the block can never be
    made whole for as long as the pin lives. The migration target in
    gup already uses GFP_USER without __GFP_MOVABLE, so a moved page
    lands in a non-movable block.

    Should defrag_mode treat MIGRATE_MOVABLE like ZONE_MOVABLE there and
    move the page out at pin time? Ideally we might want to move it back
    on unpin, but it can be done by compaction too.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/13] mm/khugepaged: drop redundant mm_struct pin in madvise_collapse()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() call is dropped to simplify the code and avoid potential issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/13] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, rather than relying on the caller to increment a shared counter. The daemon can now keep its own counter without needing to test who called the collapse function. This change simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/13] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the bitmap 'mthp_present_ptes' in the mm/khugepaged module to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed various checks. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve clarity of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/13] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and implementation of the collapse feature from the khugepaged.c file. The collapse feature is used for page migration and memory compaction. The new header file defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control parameters, as well as two constants related to page table entries. This separation improves code organization and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/13] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct called collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller before asking for a collapse. The policy includes limits on missing, swapped-out or shared PTEs in a window, as well as other settings such as whether to look at used ranges and how to handle MADV_FREE'd pages. The patch replaces scattered tests throughout the collapse path with reads from the collapse_policy struct, simplifying the code and removing the need for khugepaged to look up who called it. The policy is filled once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the call to collapse_file() from collapse_scan_file() to collapse_single_pmd(). review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledges David's feedback about virtual address scanning not being the best way to collapse page cache, but considers it out of scope for this patchset

Author explained that collapse_single_pmd() dropping the lock requires knowing which lock the caller took, and proposed adding a flag to indicate this, similar to the existing lock_dropped bool.

The author agrees that khugepaged has worked since a specific commit to walk tables under one hold, giving the lock up only to collapse, and confirms this behavior will be kept in the patch series.

Author responded to David's feedback by explaining that their version of the patch has a lower overhead than the original, citing measurements on a production config and arguing that the additional cost is acceptable given the bounded nature of the scan.

Author responded to David's feedback by explaining that khugepaged's scan rate is a critical concern for their use case, and they cannot afford to sacrifice it for the sake of having a single entry point into the engine.

Author acknowledges the appeal of a single entry point but disagrees that it's worth the cost, specifically citing negative impacts on locking and scan rate.
review_comments.raw_body:
Right on both.

As I mentioned before, virtual address scanning might not be the best
way to collapse page cache.

We might want to start from inodes on superblocks that have large folios
enabled.

But it is out of scope for the patchset.

---

That is the reason the caller owns the lock here.

On top of this series I have khugepaged scanning under the per-VMA lock:
the scan asserts whatever lock the caller holds, the caller does
vma_end_read() before the run, and the run takes the locks it needs
itself.

Neither the scan nor the run changed for it.

With collapse_single_pmd() dropping the lock, it has to know which lock
the caller took. process_madvise() on another process's mm cannot move
to the VMA lock: untagged_addr_remote() asserts mmap_lock, so a remote
MADV_COLLAPSE keeps it while a local one and khugepaged move on.

The single call would need a flag saying which lock to drop. That is
the lock_dropped bool again, pointing the other way.

---

Yes, we should.

Walking the tables under one hold and giving the lock up only to
collapse is how khugepaged has worked since ba76149f47d8 ("thp:
khugepaged").

The bool is just how that signal got plumbed when MADV_COLLAPSE arrived
in 50ad2f24b3b4, and it has already cost one bug, 5a62019807da
("mm/khugepaged: fix issue with tracking lock").

This series removes the bool and keeps the behaviour.

---

The rwsem and the VMA lookup are not the only cost.

In your version every table is a visit to the mm: unlock,
khugepaged_mm_lock, back through khugepaged_do_scan(),
khugepaged_mm_lock again, a trylock and a VMA walk, for a scan that on
memory already huge is one pmd read.

I measured your prototype against patch 9 as posted, both on a production
config, 8G of anonymous memory already collapsed, scan_sleep_millisecs 0,
pages_to_scan 65536, PMD order only, five runs each, medians:

                                     as posted    yours
  khugepaged, nothing to collapse:
    full passes over 8G in 20s         251,180    55,477
    khugepaged CPU                        100%      100%
    cost per refused table               19 ns     88 ns
  MADV_COLLAPSE, already huge:
    512M per call, p50                  3.8 us   17.4 us
    2M per call, p50                    703 ns    703 ns
  tables walked in full then refused
    (max_ptes_none 0), passes in 20s       803       836

On being nice to the rest of the system: the scan is already bounded.
The read hold ends after pages_to_scan worth of progress. We already
have properly sized scan batching in place.

---

khugepaged matters. We run it across the fleet, and its scan cost is
what decides how aggressive we can afford to be with it. I am not
giving up scan rate to keep one entry point into the engine.

For a single PMD there is no difference either way. For a range, today a
MADV_COLLAPSE over memory that is already huge walks it without letting
go of the lock at all; in your version it relocks and revalidates for
every table, and tells madvise_walk_vmas() to look the VMA up again.

---

I see the appeal of the single entry point for the collapse engine. I do.

But it costs us on both the locking picture and the scan rate. That
does not work for me.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/13] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the kernel handles memory collapsing by allowing it to work out the allowed orders for a VMA only once per VMA, rather than once per PTE table. This is done by passing the mask of allowed orders from collapse_possible_orders() directly to the functions that need it, and sampling it once per VMA instead of once per table. The patch also ensures that changes to hugepage_vma_revalidate() are properly handled under the lock that produced the mask.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 12/13] mm/collapse: declare the collapse interface in collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch declares the collapse interface in collapse.h, which includes functions and variables related to collapsing huge pages. The interface is designed to be used by a caller that holds the mmap_lock for reading, and it involves three main steps: setting up control, scanning PTE tables, and running the collapse. The patch also renames hugepage_vma_revalidate() to collapse_vma_revalidate() and adds documentation comments to explain the purpose and behavior of each function. This is a preparation step for implementing MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

[ This is the first of the cleanups I said I would front-load ]

There is no line between the collapse engine and the callers that ask for
a collapse.  khugepaged.c holds both, and they reach into each other.

 - Sixteen tests through the collapse path read cc->is_khugepaged to work
   out what they are allowed to do, when every one of those decisions was
   made by the caller before it asked.

 - collapse_single_pmd() does both halves of a collapse behind one call and
   drops mmap_lock somewhere in the middle.  Which of its paths dropped it
   is not something a caller can see, so it hands back a bool and the
   caller keeps track.

 - MADV_COLLAPSE's implementation -- the walk over the user's range, the
   per-PMD loop, the errno translation -- sits in khugepaged.c, which is
   the daemon's file.

So: draw the line.  State what a caller allows in a policy, split the call
in two with the lock as the boundary, and move the syscall to madvise.c.
What the engine offers is then three calls, with the lock state written
down against each, and a policy the caller fills for itself:

    collapse_control_init(cc)         once, before the first table
    collapse_policy_*(&cc->policy)    what this caller allows
    collapse_scan_pmd(vma, addr, ...) per table, under mmap_lock
    collapse_run_pmd(mm, addr, ...)   when a scan found work, no mmap_lock

The engine stays in khugepaged.c for now; what changes is that it has an
interface, and that neither half has to ask about the other.  madvise.c
gains the operation it should have had all along.

Changes since v3
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260916093145.4022188-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 5: the PTE limits come as two sets, struct collapse_limits for a
   PMD-sized window and one for anything smaller, and the strict_sub_pmd
   flag goes.  The warning for a max_ptes_none between 0 and the maximum
   moves to where khugepaged fills its policy.  The fields only one side
   reads are prefixed anon_ or file_.  collapse_policy_forced() is
   collapse_policy_madvise() (David).

 - Patch 8 is new: collapse_file() is called from collapse_single_pmd()
   rather than from inside collapse_scan_file(), so the file scan stops at
   the decision before the scan/run split.  The writeback retry and the
   tracepoint change move into it, so patch 9 is only the split (David).

 - Patch 9: no collapse_control_release().  It had nothing to release in
   this series; it comes back with the engine, where init allocates.  The
   check that the last scan was run stays at the top of collapse_scan_pmd()
   (David).

 - Patch 10: the changelog says why the lock boundary belongs to the
   caller (David).

 - Patch 11: both callers pass their TVA type as the literal it is rather
   than reading it back from the policy (David).

 - Patch 12: kerneldoc on every function collapse.h declares (David).

 - Acked-by from David Hildenbrand on 1-4, 6 and 7; Reviewed-by from
   Baolin Wang on 10.  Reviewed-by dropped from 5 and 9, which changed.

Changes since v2
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260910120238.2529819-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 8: the file scan returns SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE as it is and
   the run is handed what the scan returned, so it goes straight to
   retracting the PTE table when it sees it.  The scan_retract_only flag
   and the result round trip go, and the two copies of the file put become
   one helper (Zi).  Patches 9-12 follow the new signature.

 - Patch 8: mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() read the orders and
   the referenced and swapped-out counts from collapse_control instead of
   taking them as arguments (Baolin).

 - Patch 11: each interface function is documented where it is defined,
   with the lock state on entry and exit.  The overview in collapse.h
   stays (Zi).

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan on 8 and 9, and from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang
   on 5 and 10.

Changes since v1
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/cover.1788533997.git.kas@kernel.org/

 - Rebased onto mm-new with Vernon Yang's tracepoint fixes in it.  Patch 8
   no longer merges the two calls to each scan tracepoint, since the base
   already has one; its changelog now says what the status field reports.

 - Patch 3: nr_occupied_ptes is nr_eligible_ptes, and the mthp_collapse()
   comment counts eligible PTEs too (Zi, Baolin).

 - Patch 4: no comments on the two constants (Baolin).

 - Patch 5: one line per policy field (Baolin).

 - Patch 8: the file side is split like the anonymous one (Zi).
   collapse_scan_file() runs under mmap_lock in the scan and only reads;
   collapse_file() runs in the run.  See Behaviour below.

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang on 1-4, 6 and 7.

Patches
=======

The first three stand alone and can be taken separately:

  1  drop the mmgrab() MADV_COLLAPSE has held since 7d8faaf15545
  2  count collapses in khugepaged's own walk, where the daemon's
     bookkeeping belongs
  3  rename cc->mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes, which is what a set
     bit means

Then the interface, in order:

  4  add collapse.h, and move enum scan_result, struct collapse_control
     and the two constants into it
  5  struct collapse_policy, filled by the caller; the is_khugepaged
     tests become field reads, and the flag goes
  6  drop collapse_possible(), a wrapper that only turns a mask into a bool
  7  collapse_control_init_scan() is a per-table reset, so name it
     collapse_scan_reset()
  8  call collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd(), so the file scan
     stops at the decision
  9  give the scan and the collapse a function each: collapse_scan_pmd()
     and collapse_run_pmd()
 10  open-code the entry point that joined them, so each caller owns the
     lock across the boundary and the bool goes
 11  work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA, not once per table
 12  declare the three calls in collapse.h, with the lock rules
 13  MADV_COLLAPSE moves to madvise.c

Behaviour
=========

No functional change is intended.  Nothing here changes which tables get
collapsed, into what, or what MADV_COLLAPSE returns.  The tracepoints are
the one place a change can be seen from outside; the rest is where work
happens, not what it does.

 - Patches 8 and 9: mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd
   fire before the collapse rather than after it.  For an accepted table
   their status field reads SCAN_SUCCEED, where it used to carry what the
   collapse made of the table; that is now for mm_khugepaged_collapse_file
   and mm_collapse_huge_page to report.

Four things move that a reader should not have to find in the diff:

 - Patch 5: khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, so the
   max_ptes_* limits and the defrag setting behind the allocation mask are
   sampled once per pass rather than once per table.  A knob written
   mid-pass takes effect on the next pass instead of the next table.

 - Patch 8: the writeback retry re-runs collapse_file() alone, where it
   used to rescan the page cache first.

 - Patch 9: the file scan runs under mmap_lock, where before the lock was
   given up first.  A file table the scan refuses no longer costs
   khugepaged an unlock, a trip back through khugepaged_do_scan(), a
   relock and a VMA lookup; only a table it goes on to collapse does.

 - Patch 11: which orders a table is scanned for is sampled once per VMA
   rather than once per table.  It cannot widen what a collapse does; the
   order is tested again under the lock the collapse retakes.

For an anonymous table, and for a file table that gets collapsed, the lock
is given up and taken again at exactly the points it was before; the only
difference is that the caller is the one doing it.

DEBUG_VM config, in the five forms run_vmtests.sh runs it.  Every patch
builds, CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE=n included.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the tight coupling between the users of collapse and its machinery in khugepaged.c, agreeing to separate them by introducing a new header file mm/collapse.h that defines common types and constants used by both sides. This change is non-functional.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the complexity of collapse_single_pmd() by splitting it into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The new functions are designed to work together, with collapse_scan_pmd() scanning for potential collapses and collapse_run_pmd() performing the actual collapse. The author also moved the anonymous scan under mmap_lock with the file scan, reducing the number of times the lock is taken.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed David Hildenbrand's concern about the PTE limits being set differently for PMD and sub-PMD windows by introducing a new struct collapse_policy that allows callers to specify their own policy, including PTE limits. The khugepaged code will fill in this policy once per scan pass, while MADV_COLLAPSE will do so once per call. This change does not alter the behavior of khugepaged but rather simplifies the logic by removing the need for the collapse code to look up who called it.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) noted that the patch changes the behavior of khugepaged by sampling max_ptes_* limits and defrag setting once per pass instead of on every table, which is a change in behavior. He also acknowledged two other changes as not actually required for the original call to collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd().

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Andrew Morton requested that the collapse engine be separated from its callers, specifically suggesting that khugepaged.c hold only one half of a collapse and that the other half be moved to madvise.c. He proposed drawing a clear line between the two by introducing an interface for the engine and splitting the call into three parts: initialization, policy setting, and scanning/running.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Zi Yan noted that the original patch did not properly separate the scanning and running of collapses, with collapse_single_pmd() doing both jobs in the middle of a function. He suggested splitting this into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd(), which scans one table, and collapse_run_pmd(), which does the actual collapse work.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/2] iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Add a cmdq_max_n_shift module parameter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new module parameter, cmdq_max_n_shift, which allows users to cap the command queue depth as a logarithmic value of the number of entries. The default value is set to the hardware maximum, but can be overridden by setting this parameter. This change aims to provide more flexibility and control over memory allocation for systems with multiple SMMUv3 instances or tight memory budgets.

review_comments.author: Nicolin Chen
review_comments.summary: Applied the patch and added Tested-by and Reviewed-by tags. The change looks good to me.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Sep 25, 2026 at 03:15:29PM +0100, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
> 
> The command queue depth comes straight from the maximum the hardware
> advertises in IDR1, which reaches megabytes of coherent DMA per queue.
> A system with several SMMUv3 instances pays that per instance, and the
> Tegra241 CMDQV pays it again for every VCMDQ it preallocates.
> 
> Queue depth only bounds how many commands may be in flight before a sync.
> A machine driving a handful of devices, or one with a tight memory budget,
> has no use for the maximum, and no way to say so.
> 
> Add cmdq_max_n_shift, a cap on the depth given as the log2 of the entry
> count, the form the hardware itself takes in the LOG2SIZE field of
> CMDQ_BASE. It defaults to the largest depth the driver allocates, so an
> unset parameter changes nothing. Decide the depth in
> arm_smmu_cmdq_max_n_shift(), which applies the parameter to the IDR1
> value, so the queue is allocated at the requested size. The Tegra241 CMDQV
> sizes its VCMDQs from IDR1 itself, so route that through the same helper.
> 
> Floor the request at one page worth of entries. Without the floor, a small
> request trips the CMDQ_BATCH_ENTRIES check in arm_smmu_device_hw_probe()
> and the SMMU fails to probe. The floor also costs nothing: coherent DMA is
> page granular, so a shallower queue occupies the same memory as one that
> fills the page.
>

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series makes the queue depths in the ARM SMMUv3 IOMMU tunable, allowing them to be adjusted based on system requirements. The queues are currently sized from the IDR1 maximum and allocated at probe, which can consume megabytes of memory per queue per SMMU instance. In a kdump kernel, this can lead to out-of-memory errors due to limited crashkernel reservations. The patch series introduces a module parameter cmdq_max_n_shift that allows the command queue depth to be adjusted, and applies it in non-kdump kernels. This reduces the memory consumption of the queues from megabytes to kilobytes, allowing kdump kernels to save vmcores successfully.
